title: The surveyor's week, and twelve coins on the balance
summary: A traverse across the whole country, one climb per province, untimed and spread over the week with the journal open. Then the season's three tools mixed into peaks with nothing labelled, one quiet afternoon of your own surveying, and the month's monster given every day it needs.
materials: field journal, pencil, ruler and graph paper
twelve matching coins and the two-pan balance, or the coat hanger build

problems.prompt: In your head, no pencil. Of the numbers 1 to 20, how many are not multiples of 3?
explanation: Counting the ones you do not want is the shorter job here.
The multiples of 3 up to 20 are 3, 6, 9, 12, 15 and 18. That is six of them.
Twenty numbers, six crossed off, fourteen left.
problems.useAgain: when the thing you are asked to count is messy and the thing you are not asked to count is tidy.
hints: Do not hunt for the numbers that are not multiples of 3. Hunt for the ones that are.
Count up in threes from 3 and stop before you go past 20.
problems.socraticHint: Which of the two lists would be quicker to write out, and does the question care which one you write?

variant.prompt: In your head. Of the numbers 1 to 30, how many are not multiples of 4?

problems.prompt: In your head, no pencil. About how many seconds are there in a four hour window?
explanation: An hour is 60 minutes and a minute is 60 seconds, so an hour is 60 times 60.
Six sixes are 36, so 60 sixties is 3,600.
Four of those is about 14,000. The 240 is minutes, not seconds.
problems.useAgain: when a question says about how many and the numbers are easy to nudge into round ones.
hints: Work out one hour in seconds before you touch the four.
Multiply the small numbers first, then put the zeros back on.
problems.socraticHint: One of the wrong answers is the right answer to a slightly different question. Which one, and which question?

variant.prompt: In your head. About how many seconds are there in a two hour window?

problems.prompt: In your head. Which whole number is the square root of 50 closest to?
explanation: 7 times 7 is 49 and 8 times 8 is 64, so the root sits between 7 and 8.
50 is one above 49 and fourteen below 64, so it hugs the bottom of that gap.
That makes the root a whisker over 7.
problems.useAgain: when a root is not exact and you need to place it between two whole numbers.
hints: Name the two square numbers 50 sits between before you guess anything.
Ask how far 50 is from each of those squares, not how far apart the two roots are.
problems.socraticHint: Is 50 nearer the bottom of the gap between 49 and 64, or nearer the top, and how can you tell without a pencil?

variant.prompt: In your head. Which whole number is the square root of 90 closest to?

problem.prompt: The Expedition floor plan has five stations: the kitchen, the porch, the table, the whiteboard and the laptop. Corridors join the kitchen to the porch, the kitchen to the table, the kitchen to the whiteboard, the porch to the table, the porch to the whiteboard, the table to the whiteboard, and the whiteboard to the laptop. You want a route that walks every corridor exactly once. What is the smallest number of brand new corridors you would have to add to make such a route possible?
explanation: Count the corridors meeting at each station: kitchen 3, porch 3, table 3, whiteboard 4, laptop 1.
The one-stroke rule allows no odd stations or exactly two, because a station you merely pass through spends corridors in pairs.
Four are odd here, which is two too many, so no route exists yet.
One new corridor flips both stations it touches. Join the kitchen to the laptop and only the porch and the table stay odd, which is allowed, so one is enough and none is not.
The walk then has to start at the porch and end at the table, or the other way round.
problem.useAgain: when a question asks whether every path, street or corridor can be covered exactly once.
hints: Do not try to trace a route yet. Count how many corridors meet at each station.
Ask how many stations have an odd count, and what number of odd ones the rule actually allows.
problem.socraticHint: When you add one corridor, how many stations does it change, and does it make each of them more odd or less odd?

variant.prompt: A different plan, five stations A, B, C, D and E, with corridors joining A to B, B to C, C to A, C to D, D to E and E to C. What is the smallest number of new corridors you would have to add so that every corridor can be walked exactly once?

steps.title: The surveyor's week: how to sit the traverse
steps.body:
A traverse is not a summit. It is the long walk from peak to peak along a ridge, where the work is not one hard move but staying steady over eight of them without coming off.

Eight climbs, one for each province of the country you have spent a year crossing. Slope and the law of a line. Linear equations. Inequalities. Angles and polygons. Distance on the grid. Powers of ten. The three middles. Counting. Square roots are not given a climb of their own because they turn up inside the distance one and again in the warm-up, doing the last step of somebody else's work, which is exactly where they belong.

Five rules, and they are the whole method.

Spread it across the week. This is not one sitting. Two climbs on Monday and two on Tuesday is a better traverse than eight in one afternoon, because the point is whether the ground holds after a night's sleep, not whether you can sprint.

No clock. None. Not a sand timer, not a phone. The only clock in this season belongs to three dawn mornings, and it does not come in here.

Field journal open. Every climb gets working on the page, not just an answer: what you noticed, what you tried first, and the drawing if there was one. An answer with no working is a peak you cannot show anybody.

Order is yours. Read all eight first, start with the friendliest, and put a small circle beside anything that stalls you so you can come back along the ridge for it later. A peak circled and returned to is climbing. A peak stared at for twenty minutes is standing still.

Mark each one honestly when it is done: got it, got it but was unsure, or did not get it. The middle mark is the one people skip and it is the most useful of the three. Nothing here is timed and nothing here is scored, which is precisely what makes an honest mark cheap to write.

And the peaks after the traverse are deliberately not labelled. Euler, the extremal principle and the smallest criminal are all in there, and nothing tells you which peak wants which tool. Working that out is most of the climb, and it is the difference between owning three tools and owning one habit.

steps.title: The traverse: eight climbs, one per province

problems.prompt: A straight line passes through the points (0, 12) and (4, 32). Write it in the form y = mx + b, then use it. What is y when x is 7?
explanation: The point at x equals 0 hands you b, because that is where the line crosses. So b is 12.
From x 0 to x 4 the line climbs 20, and 20 over 4 steps is 5 for one step across. That is m.
So y equals 5x plus 12, and at x equals 7 that is 35 plus 12, which is 47.
problems.useAgain: when two points are given and you need the whole line rather than just those two.
hints: One of the two points is doing a job the other one cannot. Which one gives you b with no work?
Find how far the line climbs for one single step across before you go anywhere near x equals 7.
problems.socraticHint: How much does y change when x goes up by exactly one, and which part of the line's law is that number?

variant.prompt: A straight line passes through (0, 7) and (5, 27). What is y when x is 9?

problems.prompt:
Zara solved 3(x - 4) = 5x + 2 like this:
Line 1: Open the bracket: 3x - 12 = 5x + 2.
Line 2: Move the 3x to the right side: -12 = 5x + 2 + 3x, which is -12 = 8x + 2.
Line 3: Subtract 2 from both sides: -14 = 8x.
Line 4: Divide both sides by 8: x = -1.75.
Which line is wrong?
explanation: Line 2 is wrong: moving the 3x across the equals sign means subtracting it, turning 5x into 5x minus 3x, not 5x plus 3x.
Line 1 is correct: opening the bracket really does give 3x minus 12 on the left.
Lines 3 and 4 are legal moves. They are just legal moves made on the wrong equation Line 2 left behind.
Done correctly, -12 = 5x + 2 - 3x gives -12 = 2x + 2, then -14 = 2x, so x = -7, not -1.75.
problems.useAgain: when the same letter sits on both sides of an equation and has to move across the equals sign.
hints: A term does not keep its sign when it moves from one side of the balance to the other.
Check what happens to the letter's total pile size after the move, not just where it physically sits.
problems.socraticHint: If you did the same move on both sides at once instead of moving a term across, would the result look the same?

variant.prompt:
Noah solved 2(x - 5) = 4x - 6 like this:
Line 1: Open the bracket: 2x - 10 = 4x - 6.
Line 2: Move the 2x across: -10 = 4x - 2x - 6, which is -10 = 2x - 6.
Line 3: Add 6 to both sides: -4 = 2x.
Line 4: Divide both sides by 2: x = 2.
Which line is wrong?

problems.prompt: Solve -4x + 3 > 19. Negative whole numbers count here. What is the largest whole number x that makes it true?
explanation: Take 3 off both sides: minus 4x is greater than 16.
Divide by minus 4. Dividing by a negative turns the number line around, so the sign has to turn with it: x is less than minus 4.
The whole numbers below minus 4 start at minus 5, so minus 5 is the largest that works. Stopping at minus 4 gives exactly 19, and 19 is not greater than 19.
problems.useAgain: when solving an inequality makes you divide or multiply by a negative number.
hints: Get the x term on its own first and leave the minus sign sitting on it for now.
When you divide both sides by a negative, one thing in the statement has to change. Find it before you write anything.
problems.socraticHint: Put your boundary number itself back into the original line. Does it actually work, and what does that tell you about which side of it to take?

variant.prompt: Solve -3x + 5 > 20. What is the largest whole number x that makes it true?

problems.prompt: Every interior angle of a regular polygon measures 156 degrees. How many sides does it have? Write the reason beside each step in your journal.
explanation: The angles inside a polygon with n sides add up to (n minus 2) times 180.
It is regular, so the total is also n copies of 156.
Set them equal: 156n is 180n minus 360, so 24n is 360 and n is 15.
A second route: each outside angle is 24, and outside angles always add to 360, so 360 over 24 is 15 again.
problems.useAgain: when a geometry answer is only worth as much as the reason you can write next to it.
hints: You already know what all the angles inside a polygon add up to. Start from that, not from a picture.
Write the total two ways, once with the formula and once as n copies of 156, and put them equal.
problems.socraticHint: As the inside angle creeps closer to 180, does the polygon get more sides or fewer, and does 156 feel like a lot or a few?

variant.prompt: Every interior angle of a regular polygon measures 150 degrees. How many sides does it have?

problems.prompt: On the coordinate grid, how far is it in a straight line from (2, 3) to (14, 8)?
explanation: Across is 12 and up is 5. Build that right triangle.
The distance is the long side, so its square is 144 plus 25, which is 169.
The root of 169 is 13. The triangle from week 6 and the root from week 5, doing one job together.
problems.useAgain: when two points on a grid need a straight-line distance rather than a walk along the streets.
hints: Do not reach for a formula. Draw the across and the up as two sides of a right triangle.
Square both of those sides and add them before you go looking for any answer.
problems.socraticHint: Would the distance change if you walked the up first and the across second, and what does that tell you about the triangle?

variant.prompt: On the coordinate grid, how far is it in a straight line from (1, 2) to (9, 17)?

problems.prompt: Multiply 3 times 10 to the power 5 by 4 times 10 to the power negative 2. Written as a number between 1 and 10 times a power of ten, what is the power?
explanation: Fronts and tens are two jobs. 3 times 4 is 12, and the powers add, so 10 to the 5 times 10 to the minus 2 is 10 to the 3.
That gives 12 times 10 to the 3, which is true but not allowed, because the front number has to be under 10.
12 is 1.2 times 10, so slide one notch: 1.2 times 10 to the 4. The power is 4, and the trap is writing 3 and stopping.
problems.useAgain: when two numbers in scientific notation are multiplied and the front number lands outside 1 to 10.
hints: Treat the front numbers and the powers of ten as two separate jobs that meet at the end.
Before you write the power down, check whether your front number is still under 10.
problems.socraticHint: Is 12 allowed to be the front number, and if it is not, where does the spare ten have to go?

variant.prompt: Multiply 8 times 10 to the power 5 by 5 times 10 to the power negative 9. Written as a number between 1 and 10 times a power of ten, what is the power?

problems.prompt: Suppose a week of dawn readings, in degrees, came out as 12, 11, 13, 12, 10, 11 and 61, where the 61 is a real entry from the morning the thermometer was left in the sun. What is the median?
explanation: In order: 10, 11, 11, 12, 12, 13, 61. Seven readings, so the middle is the fourth.
The fourth is 12, so the median is 12.
The mean is 130 over seven, about 18.6, which is warmer than six of the seven mornings were.
One strange reading dragged the mean somewhere no morning ever was. The median did not move.
problems.useAgain: when one pile of data has an odd entry in it and you have to choose which middle to report.
hints: Order the readings before you do anything else. A median means nothing until the list is sorted.
Count how many readings there are, then work out which position along the list is the middle one.
problems.socraticHint: If the 61 had been 601 instead, which of the two middles would move, and by how much?

variant.prompt: Suppose five readings came out as 9, 10, 48, 11 and 10. What is the median?

problems.prompt: How many of the ninety two-digit numbers have at least one digit 7?
explanation: Head on you get two overlapping piles, the ones starting with 7 and the ones ending in 7, and 77 sits in both.
So count the opposite: the two-digit numbers with no 7 anywhere.
Eight choices for the first digit, nine for the second, and eight nines are 72.
Ninety take away 72 leaves 18.
problems.useAgain: when the pile you are asked about overlaps itself and the pile you are not asked about does not.
hints: Try listing them and you will meet 77 twice. That is the signal to count the other way round.
Count the two-digit numbers containing no 7 at all, one digit position at a time.
problems.socraticHint: Which pile is easier to describe in one sentence, the numbers with a 7 in them or the numbers without one?

variant.prompt: How many three-digit numbers have at least one digit 9?

steps.title: The season's shapes measured once more, and one last simulation

problems.prompt: A triangle has vertices at (0, 0), (6, 0) and (2, 5). What is its area, in square units?
explanation: The bounding rectangle runs from x = 0 to 6 and y = 0 to 5, an area of 6 times 5, which is 30.
The base of the triangle already lies flat along the bottom edge, so only two corner triangles are left over, together totaling 15.
30 minus 15 is 15 square units.
problems.useAgain: when the season's coordinate-triangle method needs one more clean run: box it in, then subtract the leftover corners.
hints: Find the bounding rectangle's area first.
Subtract the leftover corner triangles from that total.
problems.socraticHint: Does having the triangle's base lie flat along the box's edge simplify how many corner pieces are left over?

variant.prompt: A triangle has vertices at (0, 0), (8, 0) and (3, 6). What is its area, in square units?

problems.prompt: A shipping crate is 7 cm by 4 cm by 3 cm. What is its volume, in cubic cm?
explanation: Multiply all three edges: 7 times 4 times 3.
7 times 4 is 28, and 28 times 3 is 84 cubic cm.
problems.useAgain: when the season's last volume check needs the same multiply-all-three-edges rule, unit kept honest.
hints: Multiply the length and width first.
Multiply that result by the height, keeping the unit cubic.
problems.socraticHint: After multiplying three lengths together, should the answer's unit look flat or solid?

variant.prompt: A shipping crate is 9 cm by 4 cm by 2 cm. What is its volume, in cubic cm?

problems.prompt: A book club has 6 members. How many different 2-person discussion pairs can be formed, where order does not matter?
explanation: A pair does not care which member is named first.
Counting every different unordered pair from the 6 members gives 15 possible pairs.
problems.useAgain: when the season's counting-without-order idea comes up one more time, for pairs or small teams from a group.
hints: Would naming the pair in the opposite order create a different pair?
Count every different unordered pair from the 6 members.
problems.socraticHint: After a whole season of counting groups this way, does the picking order ever end up mattering?

variant.prompt: A book club has 8 members. How many different 2-person discussion pairs can be formed, where order does not matter?

problems.prompt: A fair coin is flipped 25 times and heads comes up 14 times. What fraction of the 25 flips, in lowest terms, actually showed heads?
explanation: The simulated fraction is 14 over 25.
14/25 is already in lowest terms, since 14 and 25 share no common factor.
It sits a little above the calculated 1/2, the way any one real run tends to wobble.
problems.useAgain: when the season's last simulation-versus-calculation check compares a real tally to the chance it estimates.
hints: Write the heads count over the total number of flips.
Check whether the fraction can be simplified.
problems.socraticHint: After a season of comparing simulations to calculations, does a real run ever land exactly on the calculated chance?

variant.prompt: A fair coin is flipped 25 times and heads comes up 10 times. What fraction of the 25 flips, in lowest terms, showed heads?

steps.title: Six peaks, and nothing is labelled

problems.prompt: A drawing is all in one piece and has exactly two corners where an odd number of lines meet. Which of these is true about tracing the whole drawing without lifting the pencil, using every line exactly once?
options: It cannot be traced that way at all, whatever corner you decide to start from.
It can be traced, but only starting at one odd corner and finishing at the other.
It can be traced, and you can start wherever you like, because odd corners do not matter.
It can be traced only if you start and finish at the same corner, going right round.
explanation: Every time the pencil passes through a corner it spends two lines, one in and one out.
So a corner in the middle of the journey is even. Only the place you start and the place you stop can be odd.
Two odd corners means exactly two places allowed to be an end, so they have to be the start and the finish.
Start anywhere else and you strand yourself, because you would need a third odd corner to stop at.
problems.useAgain: when a drawing has to be traced in one stroke and you need to know where to put the pencil down.
hints: Ask what happens to the lines at a corner you merely pass through, rather than at one you stop at.
In a one-stroke trace only two places are special. Name them.
problems.socraticHint: Where in a one-stroke trace is a corner allowed to have an odd number of lines, and why only there?

variant.prompt: A drawing is all in one piece and has exactly four corners where an odd number of lines meet. Which of these is true?
options: It can be traced if you start at one of the odd corners and stop at another one.
It can be traced starting anywhere on the drawing.
It can be traced only as a closed loop back to where you started.
It cannot be traced without lifting the pencil at least once.

problems.prompt: Six dots are drawn on paper and every dot is joined to every other dot by a straight line. At how many of the dots does an odd number of lines meet?
explanation: Pick any one dot. It has to reach all the others, and there are five others, so five lines meet there.
Five is odd, and no dot is different from any other, so every dot has five.
That is all six odd. The rule allows none or two, so this one cannot be traced in a single stroke.
problems.useAgain: when you need the odd corners of a drawing and counting them one by one would take all day.
hints: Do not count the lines in the whole picture. Count only the lines meeting at one single dot.
How many other dots does one dot have to reach, and does that number depend on which dot you picked?
problems.socraticHint: What would change if there were seven dots instead of six, and which single number is doing all the work?

variant.prompt: Seven dots are drawn and every dot is joined to every other dot. At how many of the dots does an odd number of lines meet?

problems.prompt: An untimed peak. Seven different whole numbers, all bigger than nought, add up to 100. The smallest of the seven is as big as it possibly can be. What is that smallest number?
explanation: Stare at the smallest and call it s. The other six are different and bigger, so the cheapest the set can be is s, s plus 1, and on up to s plus 6.
That adds to seven lots of s plus 21, and it has to fit inside 100, so s is at most 11.
A limit is only half the job. Show 11 really happens: 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16 and 19 add to exactly 100.
The extremal move was refusing to think about the other six until the smallest one had talked.
problems.useAgain: when a question asks how big the smallest thing can be, or how small the biggest thing can be.
hints: The other six numbers cost you something the moment the smallest is chosen. Work out the cheapest they can be.
Write the cheapest possible seven numbers starting from the smallest one and add them up.
problems.socraticHint: You have found a number the smallest one cannot go past. What still has to be shown before that number is the answer?

variant.prompt: Five different whole numbers, all bigger than nought, add up to 60, and the smallest is as big as it can be. What is that smallest number?

problems.prompt: An untimed peak, and the same tool from the other end. Five friends have different whole numbers of stickers, nobody has nought, and there are 40 stickers between them. The friend with the most has as few as possible. How many does that friend have?
explanation: Stare at the biggest and call it b. The others are different and smaller, so the most the group can hold is b, b minus 1, and on down to b minus 4.
That is five lots of b less 10, and it has to reach 40, so b is at least 10.
Then show 10 really happens: 6, 7, 8, 9 and 10 add to exactly 40.
Same tool, pointed the other way. There the extreme number met a ceiling. Here it meets a floor.
problems.useAgain: when the question asks for the smallest possible largest thing, or the largest possible smallest thing.
hints: Once the biggest is chosen, the other four cannot be anything they like. What is the most they can hold?
Write the greediest possible five numbers ending at the biggest one and add them up.
problems.socraticHint: In the peak before this one the extreme number could not go past a limit. Why is the limit here a floor instead of a ceiling?

variant.prompt: Four friends have different whole numbers of stickers, nobody has nought, and there are 30 between them. The friend with the most has as few as possible. How many does that friend have?

problems.prompt: Claim: every postage amount of 8 cents or more can be paid exactly using only 3 cent and 5 cent stamps. Arrest the smallest criminal, and write the whole argument out properly.

mustMention: suppose there is a smallest amount of 8 cents or more that cannot be paid
8 is 3 plus 5, 9 is three 3s and 10 is two 5s, so the criminal is at least 11
the criminal take away 3 is smaller and still at least 8, so it can be paid
adding one 3 cent stamp back pays the criminal, so no criminal exists

explanation: Suppose the claim fails. Then among the unpayable amounts of 8 or more there is a smallest one. Call it the criminal.
Pay 8, 9 and 10 by hand first: 3 plus 5, three 3s, two 5s. So the criminal is at least 11.
Take 3 off the criminal. What is left is smaller than it and still at least 8, so it can be paid, because everything below the criminal can.
Add one 3 cent stamp to that payment and the criminal is paid exactly. It was never a criminal, so there are none at all.
problems.useAgain: when a claim is made about every number past some point and you want to prove it without checking them all.
hints: Before arguing anything, pay 8, 9 and 10 with real stamps and write the payments down.
Take 3 cents off the criminal and ask what you are allowed to say about the amount you are left with.
problems.socraticHint: Why does the argument have to pay 8, 9 and 10 by hand before it is allowed to take 3 away from anything?

variant.prompt: Claim: every whole number bigger than nought can be written as a sum of different powers of 2. Arrest the smallest criminal and write the argument out.

mustMention: suppose there is a smallest whole number that cannot be written that way
take the biggest power of 2 that is not bigger than the criminal and call it P
the criminal take away P is smaller than the criminal, so it is a sum of different powers of 2
the criminal take away P is smaller than P, so P is not already in that sum and can be added

problems.prompt: A different claim: every whole number bigger than 1 has a prime factor. You suppose n is the smallest whole number bigger than 1 with no prime factor at all, and you have just written n = a times b, where a and b are both bigger than 1 and both smaller than n. What does the argument let you say next?
options: a must be prime, because every factor of a number smaller than the criminal is itself prime.
n has no factors at all, which is exactly the contradiction the method was hunting for.
a is smaller than n, so a is not a criminal and has a prime factor, which divides n too.
b is bigger than a, so b is the one to look at, and a can be ignored from here on.
explanation: The whole power of the method sits in one word, smallest. Everything below the criminal obeys the claim.
a is bigger than 1 and smaller than n, so a has a prime factor.
a divides n, so a prime factor of a is a factor of n as well, and the criminal collapses.
The last option is a distraction. Nothing says b is bigger than a, and it would not help if it were.
problems.useAgain: when you have arrested a smallest counterexample and need to find the smaller accomplice inside it.
hints: The word doing the work is smallest. What exactly does it promise you about a?
a is a factor of n. Ask what a factor of a factor does.
problems.socraticHint: What is the one thing you are allowed to assume about every single number smaller than the criminal?

variant.prompt: Same method, a bigger claim: every whole number bigger than 1 can be written as a product of primes. You suppose n is the smallest one that cannot be, and since n is not prime you write n = a times b with both bigger than 1 and smaller than n. What comes next?
options: a and b are smaller than n, so each is a product of primes, and multiplying them writes n as one too.
n must be prime after all, because the criminal cannot be allowed to have any factors.
a and b must both be prime, since only primes can multiply together to make a criminal.
The argument stops here, because nothing at all is known about a and b once they have been written down like that.

steps.title: The surveyor's mark
steps.body:
There is one more piece of surveying this week and it is different in kind from everything else on this page, so it gets said plainly rather than slipped in quietly.

Somewhere in an ordinary afternoon, not at a summit and not in front of anybody, you sit down with the readiness check that belongs to the next real book, the one that comes after the one you have been finishing. Which check that is, and who prints it, is a decision the grown-ups are still making and it belongs to them. When they have made it, it is one printed thing and one quiet afternoon, and nothing about the rest of this week changes.

What it is. A passport check. Books that begin where the next one begins publish a short list of the things they assume a reader already owns, so that somebody who does not own them yet is not left confused for six weeks with no idea why. That is all this is. It is the door of a book you want to open, checking whether you are carrying the key.

What it is not, and this half matters more. It is not a grade. No number from it goes on a wall, into a report, or to anybody outside this house. It is not a summit, and this house has never put a test at a summit and is not about to start. It is not a comparison with any other child their age, because there is nobody else in the room. And it is not timed. Take as long as it takes, in one sitting or in two, and get up and walk about in the middle if you want to.

What happens to it afterwards is the useful part. Whatever it says goes into your own surveying data, beside the pace pages and the traverse marks, and it does exactly one job: it tells you which pages of the next book to go slowly on. A check that finds three shaky things has just saved you three arguments with a textbook in October. That is a good afternoon's work, and it is the opposite of a bad result.

And if you would rather not do it at all, say so out loud and say why. That is a real option and the grown-ups decide. This is not the sort of thing that should happen to somebody who did not agree to it.

steps.title: The twelve coins get the whole week
steps.body:
The coins came off the shelf in week 9 and this week they get every day there is.

Set it up for real. Twelve matching coins on the table, the balance built or bought, and somebody else picking which coin is the fake and whether it is a bit heavy or a bit light, so you genuinely do not know. If your balance is the coat hanger and two cups, it works fine, and it tells you which side is heavier without ever telling you by how much, which is exactly the tool the puzzle assumes.

Three weighings. Find the fake, and say whether it is heavy or light. Both halves count. A method that finds the coin but shrugs about heavy or light has not finished.

How to hunt it. Do the small versions first, with your hands, not in your head. Three coins, one fake, known heavy. Then four, then nine, still known heavy. Then go back to three coins where the fake could be either kind and see how much harder that one word makes it. Write down, after each weighing you try, the full list of stories still standing. That list is the actual thing you are shrinking, and once you are watching the list rather than the coins the puzzle changes shape.

The second half, which is the better half. Once you have a method, argue that three weighings can be enough and two never can. That is a different kind of question. It is not about coins at all, it is about how much a question can possibly tell you, and it does not need a single sum.

House rules, same as every monster. Nobody hands you the method, nobody hands you the number, and nobody drops a hint at dinner. Grown-ups who already know it are allowed to play the person who hides the coin and nothing else. Come back to it in short goes across the week rather than sitting and glaring, because this is the kind of puzzle that opens while you are doing something else. And if the week ends with it uncracked, it gets retired with honours and performed anyway, because a monster nobody solved is still a monster you can describe.

steps.title: The month 3 monster: twelve coins and three weighings

problems.prompt: Twelve coins look identical. Exactly one is fake, and it is either a little heavier or a little lighter than the rest, and nobody has told you which. You have a two-pan balance and three weighings. Find the fake and say whether it is heavy or light. Then do the harder half: argue why three weighings carry enough information to always do it, and why two weighings never can.

mustMention: the first weighing is four coins against four coins
every weighing has three possible outcomes, so three weighings separate at most twenty seven cases
twelve coins each either heavy or light makes twenty four cases, and twenty four fits inside twenty seven
two weighings separate at most nine cases, which is fewer than twenty four

explanation: Number the coins 1 to 12 and weigh 1, 2, 3, 4 against 5, 6, 7, 8. Three answers, three different worlds.

If they balance, the fake is among 9, 10, 11 and 12 and the other eight are true. Weigh 9, 10, 11 against three true coins. Balanced means 12, and 12 against a true coin says which kind. A tip names the group and the kind at once, and 9 against 10 picks the coin.
If 1, 2, 3, 4 goes down, then one of 1 to 4 is heavy or one of 5 to 8 is light, and 9 to 12 are true.

Weigh 1, 2, 5 against 3, 4, 6. Balanced leaves 7 and 8, both suspected light, so weigh them and the lighter is fake. Left down leaves 1 heavy, 2 heavy or 6 light, and 1 against 2 separates them. Left up leaves 3 heavy, 4 heavy or 5 light, and 3 against 4 separates those. If 5, 6, 7, 8 had gone down, it is the same world with the two groups swapped. Weigh 5, 6, 1 against 7, 8, 2 and the third weighing follows exactly as above.
Now the counting half. A weighing answers in one of three ways, so three weighings tell apart at most 27 stories.

Twelve coins, each heavy or light, is 24 stories, and 24 fits inside 27, which is why three can work if no answer ever leaves more stories than the weighings left can carry. Two weighings answer nine ways, and nine cannot cover 24.
problems.useAgain: when a puzzle limits how many questions you get, and each question has only a few possible answers.
hints: Count the stories before you plan a single weighing. How many different endings can this puzzle have, and how many answers does one weighing give you?
Your first weighing has to leave all three of its answers with a load the last two weighings could still carry. Ask what that rules out about weighing one coin against one coin.
problems.socraticHint: Once a coin has sat on the balance and the pans came out level, what do you know about it that you can use for free later?

variant.prompt: Nine coins, one fake, and this time you are told the fake is the heavier one. You have a balance. What is the smallest number of weighings that always finds it, and why can no smaller number do the job?

mustMention: three coins against three coins, and the answer names which group of three holds the fake
nine cases and three outcomes per weighing, so two weighings separate exactly nine
one weighing separates only three cases, which is fewer than nine

steps.title: Draw the country you crossed
steps.prompt: One sheet, landscape, and draw the pre-algebra country as a map. Eight provinces with borders between them, named in your own words rather than a textbook's. Inside each province write the week you crossed it, one sentence saying what that province actually does for you, and your honest mark from the traverse. Then draw the roads: at least four arrows of ink between provinces where one of them only works because you already had the other, and write on each road what travels along it. Last, at the bottom, name the two provinces you would want a second look at before October and say why those two.

steps.title: Explain back
steps.prompt: Record yourself teaching the seven numbers that add to 100, to somebody who has never heard of the extremal principle. Do the whole thing: why staring at the smallest one is the move, why the answer needs both a limit and an example that reaches it, and where somebody would go wrong. Then two more sentences. Say which of this season's three tools you would hand a friend first and why that one. Then say one true thing the three of them have in common.
